name: ls

examples.does: Long list of everything here, hidden files included
Sizes in K, M and G
Newest first, with full dates
Show the folders themselves, not what is inside them

pitfalls: ls output is for people. In scripts, use find or a shell glob instead of reading ls output.

name: cp

examples.does: Copy a file, e.g. a backup before editing
Copy a folder keeping owners, permissions and times
Ask before overwriting
Keep a numbered backup of any file it would overwrite

pitfalls: cp -r does not keep owners and permissions. Use -a for backups.

name: mv

examples.does: Rename a file
Move, asking before overwriting
Move, but never overwrite a file already there

pitfalls: Between filesystems mv copies and then deletes. A move cut off halfway can leave a partial copy.

name: rm
tasks: remove a file whose name starts with a dash

examples.does: Delete one file
Ask before deleting each file
Delete a folder and everything in it
Delete a file whose name starts with a dash

pitfalls: There is no trash on a server: deleted is gone.
A space in the wrong place (rm -r /var /log instead of /var/log) removes far more than meant. Run ls on the exact path first.

name: mkdir

examples.does: Create a folder and any missing parent folders
Create a folder with its permissions set

pitfalls: Without -p, mkdir fails if a parent folder is missing.

name: ln
tasks: switch a symlink to a new release

examples.does: Create a symbolic link
Point an existing link at a new target (switch release)

pitfalls: Without -n, ln -sf on a link to a folder puts the new link inside that folder.

name: touch
summary: Create an empty file or update its time

examples.does: Create an empty file, or update its time if it exists
Set a chosen time, e.g. for find -newer

name: find
summary: Search for files by name, size, age, owner or permissions

examples.does: Files whose name ends in .conf
Files changed in the last 24 hours
Files over 500 MB on the root filesystem only
Delete compressed logs older than 30 days
World-writable files
Files whose owner account no longer exists
Set every file under /var/www to 644

pitfalls: Put -delete last. Placed earlier, it deletes before the other tests run.
Quote patterns ('*.log'), or the shell expands them before find sees them.
Run the command without -delete first and read the list.

name: du
summary: Disk space used by files and folders

examples.does: Total size of one folder
Size of each folder in /var, biggest last
The 20 biggest files and folders in /var/log
Number of files in each folder (when df -i shows inodes running out)

pitfalls: A deleted file that a process still holds open uses space that du cannot see. Find it with: sudo lsof +L1

name: df
summary: Free and used space per filesystem

examples.does: Space on every mounted filesystem
Same, with the filesystem type
Inodes: a disk can be full of small files while space is left
Chosen columns, without memory filesystems

pitfalls: ext4 keeps about 5% for root by default, so Use% can reach 100% for normal users while Avail is still above 0 for root.

name: stat
summary: Details of a file: owner, permissions, size, times

examples.does: Owner, permissions, size and times
Permissions as a number, with owner and group
The filesystem holding a path: type, block size, free blocks and inodes

name: file
summary: What kind of file something is
tasks: what filesystem is on a partition

examples.does: What kind of file it is
What is on a disk or partition, e.g. an ext4 filesystem

name: cat

examples.does: Print a file (here: which Ubuntu release this is)
Show hidden characters: tabs as ^I, Windows line ends as ^M
Number the lines

pitfalls: For long files use less; cat floods the terminal.

name: less
summary: Read a long file one screen at a time

examples.does: Read a file. / searches, n finds the next match, q quits
Don't wrap long lines (scroll sideways with the arrow keys)
Follow new lines like tail -f. Ctrl-C stops following, q quits

name: head
summary: The first lines of a file

examples.does: The first 20 lines
The first 200 bytes

name: tail
summary: The last lines of a file, or follow it live

examples.does: The last 50 lines
Follow new lines as they arrive (Ctrl-C stops)
Follow, and keep following after the log is rotated
Everything from line 2 on (skip a header)

pitfalls: tail -f stops showing new lines when logrotate replaces the file. Use -F.

examples.does: Number of lines (here: accounts)
Number of running processes
Changes between two files, + added and - removed
Compare two folders file by file
Only name the files that differ
